children.name: The Early Warning System
children.blurb: An early warning system tracks indicators that predict whether a student is falling off track, such as attendance, behavior incidents, and course performance, reviewed weekly or monthly.

children.name: Live Formative Checks
children.blurb: A live formative check is a quick question asked during a lesson, on a mini whiteboard or in a short online poll, that shows a teacher whether students understand before the class moves on.

children.name: Readiness Estimates
children.blurb: Readiness estimates are predictions drawn from benchmark results about which students are likely to pass state tests.

children.name: Benchmark and Item Analysis
children.blurb: Benchmark and item analysis is the practice of using periodic benchmark assessments and question level results to see how students are progressing and where instruction may need to change.

children.name: Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency
children.blurb: Growth data shows how much students have learned over time, while proficiency data shows where they stand against a standard, and both matter because a school with students starting far behind may show strong growth while proficiency stays low.

children.name: Reporting to Families
children.blurb: Reporting to Families is about giving families clear, timely information about their child's progress so they can help.

children.name: Student Self Assessment
children.blurb: Student self assessment is when students judge their own work against clear criteria and set their own goals for improvement, rather than waiting for a teacher or a tool to tell them what to fix.

children.name: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
children.blurb: This idea is that tests alone cannot show everything students know and can do, so schools should also use portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessments.

children.name: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
children.blurb: AI has changed what some assessments can tell teachers, because a take home essay or problem set may now show what a tool can do rather than what a student can do.

children.name: Survey Analysis for School Improvement
children.blurb: Survey analysis for school improvement means using surveys of students, families, and staff to see experiences that test scores cannot show, then grouping open responses into themes with AI features in spreadsheet tools.

children.name: Building Data Skills in Staff
children.blurb: Building data skills in staff means training teachers and leaders to read assessment data well, including its uncertainty and its limits.

children.name: What Data Cannot Tell You
children.blurb: What Data Cannot Tell You is the idea that numbers from tests and attendance record only a slice of a student's learning and life.

children.name: Fairness Checks
children.blurb: Fairness checks are the practice of testing whether a data system's results treat groups of students fairly, rather than assuming fairness because the inputs look balanced.

children.name: Program Evaluation
children.blurb: Program evaluation is the practice of checking whether a program or tool actually works by comparing students who used it with similar students who did not.

children.name: Board and Accountability Reports
children.blurb: Board and accountability reports are documents that school leaders must produce for governing boards, campus improvement planning and state accountability submissions, and AI can help staff draft and organize them.

children.name: Protecting Student Data
children.blurb: Protecting student data means limiting what student information is collected, who can see it, and how long it is kept.

sections.body: This part of school life is how a school gathers and uses information about what students know and how they are doing, from early warning flags to benchmark tests, growth reports, family updates, self assessment, portfolios, surveys, fairness checks, program reviews, board reports, and privacy protection. AI enters as a tool that can speed up scoring, spot patterns, and generate predictions about which students may struggle. The book describes assessment data, early warning flags, and predictions as things that can help teachers see who needs help and whether programs work, but also as things that can mislead, label, and harm when treated as certain. It also notes that traditional assessment is hard to design, gives snapshots, is not adapted to learners, fits school culture more than real-world culture, and tests skills humans now do with computers. The chapter's rule is that data starts conversations and never ends them.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that a single accuracy number makes predictions look more reliable than they are, and that when the same prediction is run many times with slightly different samples, results for individual students vary considerably, so a student flagged as at risk in one run might not be flagged in the next. It reports that machine learning can improve early warning indicators and create clear rules, but needs expertise, and that black box models invite users to read results through existing biases. It also holds that balanced group representation did not guarantee fair predictions in standardized test score prediction, and that wrong at-risk predictions often came from unforeseen life events such as family and work changes, health, and computer problems. What works is data that leads to help, with published early warning indicators, a named person who follows up on every flag, fairness checks by group, and privacy rules that remove names and identification numbers before analysis in tools not covered by a signed data privacy agreement. What does not work is the dashboard nobody acts on, data used to label rather than help, and data collected but not used, which wastes time and money. The rule it holds to is that data starts conversations and never ends them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a chain from noticing to acting to checking to reporting. A teacher or leader would start with The Early Warning System and Live Formative Checks to see who needs help and how to follow up, then use Readiness Estimates, Benchmark and Item Analysis, and Growth, Mastery, and Proficiency to understand what students know and how they are progressing. Reporting to Families and Student Self Assessment cover how information goes back to students and homes, while Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment and Assessing Learning When Students Have AI deal with richer evidence and the question of what counts as a student's own work. Survey Analysis for School Improvement and Building Data Skills in Staff support the adults who use the data, and What Data Cannot Tell You sets the limits. Fairness Checks, Program Evaluation, and Board and Accountability Reports answer whether the data leads to help and which investments work, and Protecting Student Data holds the privacy rule that runs through the whole chapter. A parent would go to Reporting to Families for how their child's progress is shared, and to Protecting Student Data for how identities are handled.
